This vignette explains the modelling vocabulary used by `compphysiol`.
It is conceptual rather than a complete function reference. For argument
details and examples, see the individual help pages.

The aim is to make explicit where common PK/PD terminology, systems biology
terminology, and the package implementation use similar words in slightly
different ways.

## Compartment model

A compartment model describes a system by splitting it into connected parts
and writing equations for how material changes over time. In PK/PD modelling,
the word "compartment" is often used very broadly: a central compartment or
peripheral compartment can mean an ODE state, a physical space, an amount of
drug in that space, or a mathematical abstraction that combines these ideas.

In `compphysiol`, these concepts are separated more explicitly. The authored
compartment model, created by `compartment_model()`, is a container for model components such as compartments,
molecules, transports, reactions, equations, observables, parameters, and
dosing events. The dynamic ODE states are usually formed later from
molecule-in-compartment combinations.

This separation is closer to systems biology modelling, where the state is
often a species in a location rather than the location alone.

Implementation anchor: `compartment_model()` creates the authored
`compphysiol_compartment_model` representation.

## Compartment

A compartment is a space, location, tissue, organ, subcellular region, or
abstract model location. It has a name and usually a volume. Examples include
`ven`, `art`, `liv`, `gut`, `cytoplasm`, and `nucleus`.

In `compphysiol`, a compartment is not itself the amount of a molecule. For
example, `liv` is the liver compartment, not "the amount of drug in the
liver". The amount of a drug in the liver is represented by the combination of
a molecule and a compartment.

Implementation anchor: compartments are represented by `compphysiol_compartments`
objects created with `compartments()` or added with `add_compartment()`.
The prefixes `Depot_` and `ReleaseRate_` are reserved for auxiliary
compartments created internally when infusion dosing is expanded during model
preparation.

## Molecule

A molecule is the entity whose amount or concentration can vary across
compartments. It may be a drug, metabolite, protein, receptor, complex,
biomarker, or other modelled substance.

Molecules can be defined for specific compartments or, when the compartment is
omitted, for all compartments. This wildcard behavior is resolved by
`wire()` before ODE generation.

Implementation anchor: molecules are represented by `compphysiol_molecules`
objects created with `molecules()` or added with `add_molecule()`.

## State

A state is a dynamic variable in the ODE system. In `compphysiol`, a state
usually corresponds to a molecule-in-compartment pair, such as drug in venous
blood or receptor in cytoplasm.

This is an important distinction from common empirical PK language, where
"compartment" often refers directly to an ODE state. In `compphysiol`, the
compartment is the location, the molecule is the entity, and the state is their
combination.

State references in expressions use DSL forms such as `a[molecule, compartment]`
for amounts and `c[molecule, compartment]` for concentrations. When the model
contains only one molecule or one compartment, shorter forms may be wired to
the full state reference.

Programmatic state objects can also carry wildcard molecule or compartment
references. An unspecified molecule or compartment is stored as
`NA` internally and is resolved by `wire()` to the corresponding molecule or
compartment names before ODE generation.

During ODE export, the integrated state representation is chosen by an export
policy rather than by the molecule-compartment identity alone. The default
policy prefers amount states when they are given directly or can be obtained
from concentration initials using a fixed or parametrized compartment volume.
If no usable volume is available and the molecule is defined by concentration
initials, the ODE state remains a concentration state. This supports pure
reaction systems without physical compartment volumes, while transports and
dosing require amount states or a volume-based conversion.

Initial values may themselves be fixed values or parameter expressions. For
example, a molecule can be initialized with a named amount or concentration
parameter rather than a numeric value. Such expressions are still attached to a
specific molecule-in-compartment state; they do not create new states. When the
parameters needed to evaluate an initial value or a volume conversion are
present in the model, `initials()` resolves the expression to a value, including
unit-aware values. When some parameters are not yet present, the unresolved
expression remains symbolic until a later boundary, such as ODE export or
simulation, where numerical solver initial values must be available.

The `initials()` helper exposes this representation choice more flexibly. It
can request amount initials, concentration initials, or fallback behavior in
either direction. ODE export currently uses the amount-preferred fallback as
its public default.

Implementation anchor: programmatic state references use the
`compphysiol_states` class and are created with `state()`.

## Domain-specific language

The domain-specific language is the small expression syntax that lets model
components refer to states, parameters, and equations while remaining ordinary
R expressions or character strings.

State references use bracket forms. `a[molecule, compartment]` refers to an
amount state and `c[molecule, compartment]` refers to a concentration state.
When the model contains enough information, shorter one-index forms can be
wired to full state references. For example, `a[drug]` can be expanded when
there is only one relevant compartment, and `a[Central]` can be expanded when
there is only one relevant molecule.

The same expression syntax is used in transport rates, reaction rates,
equations, observables, and some initial values. In user-facing constructors
and add-functions, expressions may be supplied either as ordinary R expressions
using non-standard evaluation, such as `add_observable(C = c[drug, Central])`,
or as character strings, such as `add_observable(C = "c[drug, Central]")`.

Expression-like arguments interpret bracket calls as model-state references.
For example, `a[Central]` means an amount state in the `Central` compartment
when the omitted molecule can be resolved. It is not interpreted as a numeric
object named `a` with unit `Central`.

## Unit shorthand

Units are part of the intended model semantics. Exported value-like arguments
where physical units are meaningful accept unit-aware syntax of the form
`value [unit]`, for example `100 [mg]`, `0.2 [1/h]`, or `1 [mg/L]`. The
shorthand is converted to `units` objects and can be used for compartment
sizes, molecule initial values, parameter values, dosing times, dosing
amounts, infusion rates, infusion durations, and simulation time points.

Unit-aware arguments support ordinary R arithmetic over unit expressions. For
example, `10 [mg] / 200 [g/mol]` derives an amount from a mass and molar mass,
and `30 [min] + 0.5 [h]` derives a dosing or simulation time. The same syntax
can be used directly outside unit-aware arguments (e.g., during data processing) 
by using `with_units()`.

Unit shorthand is not evaluated inside expression-like arguments such as
transport rates, reaction rates, equations, or observables. transport and
reaction `const` arguments are value-like when supplied as explicit values, so
`const = 0.2 [1/h]` is interpreted as a unit-bearing rate constant. Symbolic
constants can still be supplied through character expressions, for example
`add_transport(..., const = "k")` together with `parameters(k = 0.2 [1/h])`.
This keeps bracket syntax unambiguous: value-like `const` arguments use
brackets for units, while explicit `rate` expressions use brackets for
model-state references.

The shorthand follows ordinary R parsing rules, meaning that the unit bracket
takes precedence over arithmetic operators. For example, `1/2[h]` is parsed 
as `1 / (2 [h])`, so it means `0.5 [1/h]`, not `0.5 [h]`. Use parentheses when 
the intended order is different, for example `(1/2) [h]`.

Unit checking is a boundary behavior rather than a separate model component.
During ODE export and simulation, unit-aware model values are checked for
dimensional consistency, converted to solver-facing numeric dimensions, and
then attached back to toolbox-level simulation output where possible.

## Transport

A transport moves the same molecule from one compartment to another. It changes
location but preserves molecular identity.

In PBPK models, many physiological "flows" are represented as transports:
blood flow from arterial blood to an organ, venous return from tissue to blood,
or clearance from a compartment to a sink. A transport can be linear, through a
first-order rate constant, or nonlinear, through an explicit rate expression.

Implementation anchor: transports are represented by `compphysiol_transports`
objects created with `transports()` or added with `add_transport()`. Transport rates
may use parameters, states, and equations; during ODE export, equations can be
used to define reusable transport rate constants or rate expressions.

## Flow

"Flow" is common PBPK jargon for movement between compartments, especially
perfusion-mediated movement.

In `compphysiol`, use "transport" for compartment-to-compartment movement
unless the code is explicitly discussing a physiological flow parameter such
as `Qliv`.

## Reaction

A reaction changes molecular identity or stoichiometry. For example, a reaction
may convert drug to metabolite, bind ligand and receptor into a complex,
synthesize a molecule, or degrade a molecule.

This differs from a transport: a transport moves a molecule between
compartments while preserving molecular identity, while a reaction transforms
one set of localized state participants into another. A participant is a
molecule in a compartment, such as ligand in plasma or receptor on a membrane.
The common same-compartment reaction is the shorthand case where all
participants are localized in one compartment. Cross-compartment reactions are
used when the reacting participants are localized in different compartments,
such as ligand in plasma binding to receptor in a membrane compartment to form
a membrane-localized complex.

Reactions may have multiple inputs and outputs. Their vector arguments describe
stoichiometric participants rather than vectorized creation of many unrelated
reactions. Repeated participants represent stoichiometry, for example two
copies of the same input molecule.

Reaction formulas provide a compact character-string syntax for the same
participant structure, for example `A + B -> C` or
`L[plasma] + R[membrane] -> LR[membrane]`. Unlocalized participants in a
formula have the same wildcard or `cmt`-filled meaning as separate `input` and
`output` character arguments.

Reaction rates can be represented as concentration-change rates or amount-change
rates. Explicit `rate` expressions declare this with `rate_type`. For elementary
reactions specified with `const`, the constant always has its usual mass-action
meaning; when the reaction scale is provided or unambiguous, `rate_type`
controls how the generated rate expression is presented. A concentration
representation uses concentration factors for all reactants. An amount
representation replaces one reactant concentration factor with its amount,
giving an algebraically equivalent amount/time expression.
`scale_cmt` selects the compartment supplying that amount factor, or the
compartment size used to convert a concentration rate to an amount rate.

For `const` reactions, a single-compartment reaction defaults to a concentration
rate and a cross-compartment reaction defaults to an amount rate. `scale_cmt`
is inferred when all reactants occur in one compartment. When reactants occur
in multiple compartments it must be supplied regardless of `rate_type`.
Amount-rate reactions require every participant state to be convertible to an
amount state. This makes a shared cross-compartment reaction flux explicit and
mass-conserving. Transports likewise always use amount/time rates.

The `c[]` and `a[]` state-reference forms keep their usual meaning in reaction
rates. The unit of `c[molecule, compartment]` depends on the size assigned to
that compartment: for ordinary volumetric compartments it is an amount per
volume, while for surface-like compartments it may be an amount per area. ODE
export still chooses amount states when possible and concentration states when
amount conversion is not available.

Implementation anchor: reactions are represented by `compphysiol_reactions`
objects created with `reactions()` or added with `add_reaction()`. Current reaction
support covers construction, storage, printing, wildcard wiring, and numerical
ODE export. Analytical export and unit checking for reactions are not
implemented yet.

## Equation

An equation defines an auxiliary expression. Equations are not ODE states and
are not observables by themselves.

Equations are useful for derived quantities such as physiological sums,
partitioning terms, or reusable rate expressions. In the current ODE export,
equations can be reused in transport and reaction constants and rate
expressions. Equations help keep generated ODEs readable while preserving the
symbolic structure of the model.

The symbol `t` is reserved for current model time. An equation that uses `t`,
directly or through another equation, is time dependent. For example,
`V = V0 * exp(mu * t)` defines an exponentially changing volume. ODE backends
evaluate these equations at the solver's current time. Analytical and
stochastic model conversions currently reject them explicitly.

A compartment with a time-dependent volume is represented with amount states,
so dilution or concentration caused by volume change is obtained as `amount / V(t)`
without adding an artificial amount-change term. Initial conditions are defined
at the first simulation time. A concentration initial in such a compartment is
therefore converted to an amount using the volume at that time.

Implementation anchor: equations are represented by `compphysiol_equations`
objects created with `equations()` or added with `add_equation()`.

## Observable

An observable is a quantity calculated from states and parameters after or
during simulation. It is meant to represent something that can be
reported, compared to data, or plotted, such as plasma concentration or total
amount in a tissue group.

An observable is not part of the ODE state vector. It is derived from the model
state rather than integrated as an independent dynamic variable.

ODE observable export defines equation helper variables inside observable
functions, so observables can reuse named equations, including time-dependent
ones.

Implementation anchor: observables are represented by `compphysiol_observables`
objects created with `observables()` or added with `add_observable()`.

## Parameter

A parameter is a named value used in the model. Parameters may represent
physiology, compound properties, kinetic constants, partition coefficients, or
other fixed inputs to simulation and analysis.

Parameters can be numeric, categorical, symbolic, or unit-aware. Unit-aware
parameter values use the general unit shorthand described above.
The name `t` is reserved and cannot be used for a parameter.

Implementation anchor: parameters are represented by `compphysiol_parameters`
objects created with `parameters()` or added with `add_parameter()`.

## Parameter set

A parameter set is one realized collection of parameter values. Several sets
can represent a realized population, such as individual-specific body weights,
sexes, physiological values, or compound parameters. Numeric and categorical
covariates are ordinary parameters rather than a separate component type.

A parameter-set collection contains only parameter objects and carries no
metadata about individuals or about how their values were generated. It
therefore represents a realized population, not a population distribution or
sampling model. Parameter names shared across sets must have compatible units.
Sampled populations remain unnamed and retain sampling order; names are
optional user metadata rather than generated individual identifiers. Positive
whole-number names are reserved for transient positional identifiers and
cannot be supplied explicitly.
The collection records whether every set has the same parameter schema: names,
order, value types, classes, dimensions, lengths, and units. This structural
homogeneity metadata does not imply equal parameter values or retain sampling
provenance. It allows downstream operations to validate and prepare a shared
schema once.

Implementation anchor: realized parameter sets use `compphysiol_parameter_sets`,
created with `parameter_sets()`. Subsetting with `[` retains the collection,
while `[[` extracts one `compphysiol_parameters` object.

## Dosing

Dosing describes external input into the model, such as a bolus dose or an
infusion. Doses target a molecule and compartment, either explicitly or through
wildcards that can be resolved during wiring.

Infusion dosing may create additional depot or release-rate structures during
ODE export. These are implementation devices for representing the dosing
schedule, not necessarily physiological compartments.

Implementation anchor: dosing events are represented by `compphysiol_dosing`
objects created with `dosing()` or added with `add_dosing()`.

## Observation schedule

An observation schedule specifies which named model observables to evaluate and
at which times. It has `time` and `observable` columns but no value column. A
schedule describes a design or request, rather than observed or predicted data.
Repeated rows, row order, and additional metadata columns are preserved.

Even a directly measured state quantity must be declared as a model observable
and referenced by that observable's name. Observation times are either
unit-free or carry time units.

Implementation anchor: observation schedules are represented by
`compphysiol_observation_schedule` data-frame-like objects created with
`observation_schedule()`.

## Observation data

Observation data associate values with an observation schedule. They have the
canonical columns `time`, `observable`, and `value`, and may retain additional
row metadata. The representation is deliberately neutral about provenance:
values may be experimental measurements, predictions from another model,
synthetic data, or externally prepared observations.

Observation data also satisfy the observation-schedule contract, so code that only
needs evaluation points can consume it as a schedule. The explicit
`as_observation_schedule()` conversion removes the `value` column. Observable
simulation output uses the same observation data representation, allowing one
model's predictions to be supplied directly as data when calibrating another
model, provided their observable names and units are compatible.

A conditional prediction is the deterministic observable value returned by
`simulate()`. A sampled observation is a random value drawn conditionally from
an observation-level distribution around such a prediction. Both use
observation data; the class deliberately remains neutral about whether values
are measured, predicted, or synthetically sampled.

Implementation anchor: observation data are represented by
`compphysiol_observation_data` objects, which inherit from
`compphysiol_observation_schedule` and are created with `observation_data()`.

## Statistical model

A statistical model assigns probability distributions to named random
quantities. The left-hand-side name identifies either an unresolved structural
parameter in the dynamic model or a model observable. Structural-parameter
distributions describe individual variability; observable distributions
describe the probabilistic relationship between predictions and values in
observation data. The statistical model does not obtain a
population location implicitly from a fixed structural-model value.

The primary distribution families are `normal()` and `lognormal()`. Locations
and scale components may refer to statistical parameters by name or may be
fixed scalar values. Unit-bearing fixed values are retained. A normal
distribution has a mean and a standard-deviation specification. A bare
standard-deviation name or value is constant, `proportional()` means the
coefficient times the absolute resolved mean, and `combined()` initially means
the constant component plus the proportional component times the absolute
resolved mean. This additive convention is explicit; a future quadrature
convention would require a separate option.

A log-normal distribution is parameterized by its median and `sdlog`. The
median is also its geometric mean. It is not the arithmetic mean, and the API
does not accept `mean` or a raw `logmean`. For an individual parameter `CL`,
`lognormal(median = "CL_pop", sdlog = "omega_CL")` means that `log(CL)` is
normal with location `log(CL_pop)` and standard deviation `omega_CL`.

Missing locations are context-sensitive. For an observable, a missing normal
mean or log-normal median resolves to the dynamic-model prediction; in the
log-normal case the prediction is explicitly the conditional median. An
individual-level structural parameter always requires an explicit location.
Levels are otherwise inferred during validation: unresolved structural
parameters are individual-level and observables are observation-level. A name
that identifies both requires an explicit level, and fixed structural
parameters cannot initially be replaced by individual distributions.

Normal locations and constant standard deviations use the target's units.
Proportional coefficients and log-normal `sdlog` values are dimensionless.
Consequently realized structural values retain structural target units and
observations retain observable units.

Implementation anchor: `statistical_model()` creates a
`compphysiol_statistical_model` that collects unresolved distribution
specifications. `estimation_problem()` resolves their targets and levels against
the dynamic model and validates their dimensions. The optim engine currently
supports observation-level entries only; individual-level entries require a
mixed-effects-capable engine.

`correlated()` declares pairwise correlations between individual-level
parameter distributions in the same statistical model. Each declaration names
two random quantities and a fixed correlation or statistical-parameter name.
The correlation applies to the latent normal variables underlying normal and
log-normal marginals; unspecified pairs are uncorrelated. Normal marginals in a
correlated structure require a constant standard deviation rather than a
proportional or combined specification. Correlations cannot be attached to
observation-level error distributions. Because target levels are inferred from
the dynamic model, this restriction is fully checked when the statistical model
is resolved.

`sample_population()` realizes the individual-level entries as a named
collection of parameter sets. Population locations, variability parameters, and
correlation parameters are inputs to sampling but are not copied into each
realized individual. Symbolic correlations are resolved at this boundary, the
completed correlation matrix is checked for positive semidefiniteness, and
correlated latent normal draws are transformed through their marginal
distributions. Observation-level entries are ignored.

By default, sampling requires levels to have been made explicit or resolved and
selects every individual-level entry. An explicit `targets` vector can instead
identify exactly which statistical-model entries represent structural
parameters to sample. This resolves missing levels for those entries without
guessing from the availability of their population parameters; entries already
marked observation-level cannot be selected.

`sample_observations()` performs the complementary observation-level step. The
observable names represented in its prediction rows act as its internal target
set. Matching entries with unresolved levels are treated as observation-level,
entries explicitly marked individual-level are rejected, and unrelated
statistical entries are ignored. Every input row must have a matching
distribution; sampling replaces values without filtering or reordering rows.
The input prediction is always the distribution location, so explicit
observation locations are rejected. The function requires prediction-bearing
observation data, giving it an observation-data-to-observation-data
contract. Predictions in a simulation result are extracted explicitly with
`as_observables_long()` before sampling.

## Experiment

An experiment entry represents one independent individual simulation or
estimation unit. It specifies known parameters, a fixed dosing schedule, and
either an observation schedule or observation data for a model. It is separate
from the biological model. Several entries can describe different individuals,
administrations, or experimental settings for the same system.

Experiments are always represented as collections, including when there is
only one entry. Cardinality is therefore a property of the object rather than
part of its class. `experiment()` constructs a length-one collection, and
`c()` combines collections. Subsetting with `[` always retains the collection;
direct `[[` extraction is blocked so that an internal entry cannot become a
second public representation.

An optional name supplied to `experiment()` identifies its single entry.
Names can also be supplied while combining entries with `c()`. Unnamed entries
remain unnamed in storage. When a named argument to `c()` wraps a length-one
experiment that already has a name, the outer argument name replaces the stored
name. This makes the call site authoritative when assembling a collection.

Covariates such as body weight and sex are ordinary values in an experiment
entry's parameters; there is no separate subject-metadata component.
Relationships derived from covariates belong in model `Equation`s, which may
depend on both experiment parameters and shared model parameters.

The `observations` component contains either an observation schedule or
observation data. Because observation data inherit from observation schedules,
simulation can use either representation directly. Estimation additionally
requires the stored observations to contain values. Observation variability is
not part of the experiment and belongs to the statistical model used during
estimation.

An experiment has an explicit initial time, at which the model's initial
values apply. This can precede the first dose or observation. Observation and
dosing times cannot precede it. Times are either all unit-free or carry
compatible time units; hours and minutes can coexist. By default, `start = NULL`
resolves to zero in the units of the first nonempty schedule (dosing, then
observations). If both are empty, it remains automatic internally while being
displayed as zero. Its unit mode is resolved when a time-bearing component is
added or when it is combined with resolved experiments. It does not select the
earliest scheduled time: adding a later first observation does not shift when
initial values apply. Negative schedule times require an explicit earlier start.
Incompatible schedule units remain an error.

Experiment parameters are known values, fixed during the experiment. Joint
estimation keeps these separate from shared estimated parameters and rejects
overlap. General scheduled parameter changes
and time-dependent model equations are not part of the current experiment
contract. Dosing may be calculated from known experimental values before
constructing the experiment.

Current support covers construction, printing, and ODE simulation.
An experiment supplies the complete dosing schedule, replacing model-attached
dosing even when the experiment schedule is empty. Its known parameters override
model defaults. Simulation starts at the initial time and evaluates only the
scheduled observable-time pairs. Stored observation values do not affect
simulation. Collection simulation returns one simulation result. For multiple
entries, its tables carry an experiment identifier; length-one output omits
that redundant column. Experiments containing observation data can be used for
estimation.

Implementation anchor: experiments use `compphysiol_experiments` at every
length. A length-one collection is created with `experiment()` and collections
are assembled with `c()`.

An experiment collection holds several
independent individual units. The element name is the individual identifier;
unnamed elements remain accepted for workflows that do not yet assign one.
Nonempty identifiers must be unique, while any number of elements may remain
unnamed. Names are preserved when supplied but are not generated when a
protocol is extended across unnamed parameter sets. Positive whole-number names
are reserved for transient positional identifiers and cannot be supplied
explicitly.
Subsetting with `[` retains a collection and `[[` is blocked. Collections can
be combined with `c()`. Printing chooses its presentation by length: a
length-one collection shows the full experiment details, while a longer
collection shows shared and per-entry summaries.

Collections require a common time unit mode across experiments, including their
initial times: all unit-free or all in compatible time units. Parameters shared
by name must have compatible units, as must dose amounts for each shared
molecule-compartment target. Boluses and infusions are compared through their
total amounts. Compatible units are preserved, not converted in storage.
Omitted dosing targets match identically omitted targets; matching them to
explicit targets requires later model-based resolution. These checks also apply
when combining collections with `c()`.

Experiment components are modified with domain-specific verbs. Parameters can
be added with conflict checking, overlaid by name, or replaced completely;
dosing can be appended or replaced; observations and start times can be
replaced; and values can be attached to observation schedules. Scalar
components broadcast across a collection. Parameter sets expand a length-one
collection and otherwise align by effective experiment identifier, or
positionally when both collections are wholly unnamed. Callbacks receive the
current component of each experiment and return the incoming component to
which the chosen verb is then applied.

An experiment collection records whether its starts, parameter schemas,
complete parameter values, dosing schedules, observation plans, and complete
observations are each identical across all members. This homogeneity metadata
does not change the meaning or independence of the experiments. It allows
simulation and estimation implementations to prepare a shared component once
when the whole collection is homogeneous, while heterogeneous components keep
their ordinary per-experiment behavior. A false homogeneity flag means only
that not all values are identical; it does not imply that every value differs.

A shared experimental protocol can be extended across a realized population
with `overlay_parameter(protocol, population)`. The protocol supplies dosing,
observations, start, and shared parameters; each realized parameter set supplies
the individual parameters for one resulting experiment. Individual values
override protocol parameters with the same name. The explicit transformation
produces an experiment collection before simulation rather than adding a
population concept to `simulate()`.

`attach_observation_values()` transforms an observation schedule and
corresponding values into observation data. It preserves row order, duplicate
rows, units, and metadata. Bound data align by experiment identifier and must
agree rowwise on all schedule columns they share.

Simulating an experiment collection returns one simulation result. Its state
and observable tables contain an `experiment` factor whose levels follow
collection order. Supplied experiment names are used as identifiers, while
unnamed experiments receive transient one-based identifiers. The `observations()`
accessor binds stored observation schedules or data and adds an `experiment`
identifier. It uses supplied experiment names and transient one-based positions
for unnamed experiments; these identifiers are not written back to the
collection. Simulation results themselves remain separate.

Repeated occasions within an individual and state-reset semantics are outside
the current experiment contract.

## Estimation problem

An estimation problem combines a deterministic dynamic model, one or more
experiments containing observation data, explicit estimated-parameter
specifications, and a statistical model. It is engine-neutral: the same
scientific estimation specification can be evaluated by different estimation
engines without moving statistical assumptions into the compartment model.

Estimated parameters declare an initial value, optional bounds, and an internal
identity, log, or logit transformation. Units are retained at the model and
observation boundaries while optimization uses numeric internal coordinates.
Known experiment parameters cannot simultaneously be shared estimated
parameters.

Omitted bounds depend on the transformation and inherit the initial value's
units. Identity uses an unbounded interval, log uses zero as its lower bound and
has no finite upper bound, and logit uses the interval from zero to one.
Bounds are part of the parameter specification rather than the optimization
engine's control list. `L-BFGS-B` accepts effective box constraints. `Brent`
requires exactly one identity-transformed parameter with finite bounds.
Methods without native bound support accept log and logit transformations, but
reject finite optimizer-coordinate bounds not already enforced by the
transformation. Thus a log parameter with its natural `(0, Inf)` domain and a
logit parameter with its declared interval are unconstrained in optimizer
coordinates, whereas an additional finite bound requires `L-BFGS-B`.

An individual specification is a parameter specification. Named specifications are
combined with `c()` into a parameter-specification collection. Collections can be
combined again; `[` retains a collection, while `[[` extracts one specification.

Current estimation supports compartment model, process model, ODE model, and
compiled deSolve model inputs. These are model representations, not engines.
Analytical and stochastic model representations are outside the current
estimation contract. An estimation engine owns the fitting workflow and may
contain a simulation engine. The first estimation engine uses `stats::optim()`
to minimize the joint negative log-likelihood across experiments and delegates
ODE evaluation to a deSolve simulation engine. The latter can prepare either an
ODE model or a compiled deSolve model; compilation changes the representation
consumed by the same deSolve path rather than selecting another estimation
engine. An
estimation result exposes coefficients, the negative log-likelihood, population
predictions, optional individual predictions, and the native engine result.
Convergence information, residual diagnostics, objectives, and other
backend-specific quantities remain in the native engine result.
Parameter standard errors are normalized to the public parameter scale, after
accounting for optimization transformations, backend parameterizations such as
variance versus standard deviation, and solver-unit conversion. They therefore
have the same units as their corresponding estimates. Joint uncertainty is
exposed as a unitless correlation matrix in the same parameter order. This
correlation describes uncertainty among estimates; it is distinct from a
correlation between individual random effects in the statistical model.
Uncertainty entries remain missing when an engine did not calculate them or
when its covariance calculation did not cover a parameter.
For unit-bearing continuous observations, the shared negative log-likelihood is
reported on the numerical scale of the units in which the observations were
supplied. When an engine evaluates densities after converting observations to
solver units, the corresponding change-of-units Jacobian is applied before the
likelihood is exposed in the estimation result.

The nlmixr2 engine integrates mixed effects and
owns more than an outer optimization algorithm: ODE evaluation, residual
likelihoods, random-effect approximation or integration, and the estimation
algorithm belong to that engine. It therefore consumes the scientific model,
experiments, parameter specifications, and statistical model directly; it is
not an outer optimizer configured with a separate simulation engine. This is
distinct from numerical ODE simulation, where the simulation type selects ODE
semantics and a deSolve or rxode2 engine selects the interchangeable execution
backend.

The initial mixed-effects scope is FOCEi estimation with independent
individual-level random effects. Correlated random effects remain part of the
statistical-model vocabulary but are outside this first engine milestone, as
is SAEM estimation. Standard deviations in normal and log-normal distribution
specifications retain their public standard-deviation scale. At the nlmixr2
boundary, individual-level standard deviations are squared to form diagonal
omega variances; fitted omega variances are square-rooted when translated back
to the public result.

The same engine can fit a population-only problem without individual-level
random effects. This provides an independent execution path for a fixed-effects
problem that can also be fitted by the optim engine. Agreement of parameter
estimates, predictions, and likelihood values on such a problem is used as an
engine-conformance check.

A mixed-effects result distinguishes individual predictions, conditional on
the fitted random effects for each individual, from population predictions,
calculated for the typical individual with random effects set to zero. These
two explicit names are sufficient; an unqualified predictions component would
be ambiguous and is not part of the mixed-effects result contract. Prediction
tables preserve the observation rows and their order. Because a mixed-effects
fit has both levels, fitted-value extraction requires the caller to select the
population or individual prediction explicitly. An estimation without
individual effects has only one prediction level and needs no selection; for an
nlmixr2 result, the backend labels for population and individual predictions
both resolve to that same table.
Residuals are not currently normalized across engines because their definitions
depend on both the prediction level and the backend-specific residual type.

Implementation anchor: `estimation_problem()` creates
`compphysiol_estimation_problem`; `parameter_spec()` creates one
`compphysiol_parameter_spec`; `parameter_specs()` creates a collection with an
optional shared transform, and `c()` combines existing specifications into
`compphysiol_parameter_specs`; `optim_engine()` configures the optimizer and
its `deSolve_engine()`; `nlmixr2_engine()` creates
`compphysiol_nlmixr2_engine`; and `estimate()` returns
`compphysiol_estimation_result`.

## Source and sink

A source represents material entering the model from outside the explicit
compartment set. A sink represents material leaving the model. User-facing
interfaces may accept `NULL` or `""` for these cases.

Internally, source and sink compartments are represented as `NA_character_`.
This convention matters when reading or changing transport and reaction code.

## Wildcard

Some model components can omit a molecule or compartment to mean "all relevant
molecules" or "all relevant compartments". For example, a transport without a
specific molecule can apply to all molecules, and a molecule without a specific
compartment can be present in all compartments.

Wildcards make compact model definitions possible, but they also mean that the
model is not fully explicit until it has been wired.

## Wiring

Wiring resolves wildcard molecules and compartments into explicit model
components. It also expands short state references in expressions when the
model contains enough information to do so unambiguously.

`wire()` is called before ODE generation. It can also be called directly when a
fully explicit model is useful for inspection or for avoiding later changes in
interpretation as new components are added.

Implementation anchor: wiring is handled by `wire()` for
`compphysiol_compartment_model` objects.

## Model merging

Model merging combines two compartment models into one. In the
limited overlay mode, matching names are interpreted as the same modelling
entity: a compartment with the same name is the same location, a molecule with
the same name is the same substance, and a matching molecule-in-compartment
combination is the same state. If both models define the same compartment, the
compartment volume must also be the same; otherwise the two definitions do not
describe the same location and cannot be overlaid without an explicit modelling
decision.

Overlay merging is intended for combining subsystems that describe different
parts of the same model, such as an oral absorption subsystem and a systemic PK
subsystem for the same molecule. It appends model processes such as transports,
reactions, observables, parameters, and dosing events while sharing the common
state space identified by molecule and compartment names.

Overlay merging does not resolve wildcards. Wildcard molecules or compartments
remain compact, unresolved component definitions in the merged model, and their
interpretation can still change when additional molecules or compartments are
added later. Call `wire()` before or after merging when a fully explicit state
space is needed.

Overlay merging is not a renaming or copying operation. Building independent
copies of a model for multiple compounds requires explicit renaming before
merging or a separate copy/renaming helper.

Implementation anchor: `mergeModels()` combines two
`compphysiol_compartment_model` objects.

## Object construction and validity

Package constructors establish the intrinsic validity of the objects they
return. Intrinsic validity consists of facts that can be checked from the
object alone, such as its required fields, allowed values, consistent lengths,
and internal unit relationships. User-facing constructors accept convenient
input and report domain-specific errors; internal low-level constructors attach
the canonical representation and S3 classes to values that have already been
normalized.

Model-component modifiers have two construction routes. In interactive use,
named constructor arguments are forwarded to the corresponding component
constructor, for example `add_compartment(name = "central")`. In programmatic
use, an already constructed component occupies the second argument, for
example `add_compartment(compartments(name = "central"))`. The same convention
applies to compartments, molecules, transports, reactions, observables, and
equations. Supplying a constructed component together with constructor
arguments is ambiguous and rejected.

Code that receives a package S3 object trusts this intrinsic class contract.
For example, printing, subsetting, and simulation do not need to repeat every
check performed by the object's constructor. Operations that create a new
combination, such as concatenation, replacement, or adding a model component,
must establish any invariants that their result could newly violate.

Contextual compatibility is distinct from intrinsic validity and remains the
responsibility of the operation with the necessary context. Simulation must,
for example, check that an experiment's observables and dosing targets occur in
the selected model, that required parameters are available, and that values
are compatible with the solver boundary. An experiment can therefore be
intrinsically valid while being incompatible with a particular model.

Because these are S3 objects, users can manually alter attributes or otherwise
bypass the supported constructors. Consumers are not required to defend
against every such modification by rechecking the entire object. Cheap class
checks remain appropriate at public API boundaries.

Implementation convention: migrated classes use an internal
`.new_<class>()` for cheap construction and a public `<class>()` helper for
input normalization and checking. Focused helpers may check conflicts that can
be introduced by several operations, such as duplicate names during
concatenation or incompatible units across collections; consumers do not run a
general per-class validator.

## Model representations and execution

A model representation is a persistent package-owned encoding of model
structure. The authored compartment model and all representations obtained by
lowering it share a common model superclass. The authored model
retains the domain-level compartment, molecule, transport, and reaction
structure. Process, ODE, analytical, and stochastic models encode successively
more explicit mathematical forms for particular analyses.

An executable model is a persistent backend-specific representation that can
be run repeatedly. Executable models additionally share an executable-model
superclass. They do not inherit from the solver-neutral ODE-model class merely
because they contain or
were derived from one: their own structure follows a backend-specific contract.
The compiled deSolve representation and the rxode2 representation are
executable models in this category. The rxode2 representation retains generated
backend source and caches its compiled payload for repeated simulation.

An engine selects and configures how a representation is executed. Simulation
engines and estimation engines are execution strategies, not model
representations. Solver payloads, such as a deSolve derivative function,
numeric initial state, parameter vector, and event table prepared for one run,
are transient internal objects. ODE export names the transformation across this
solver boundary; it is not a public class hierarchy.

For numerical ODE simulation, `simulation_type = "ode"` selects the ODE
semantics while `deSolve_engine()` or `rxode2_engine()` selects the execution
backend. The rxode2 engine contains solver configuration; scientific model
content remains in the model representation.

Package-owned S3 classes use lower-case `compphysiol_`-prefixed names to avoid
global S3 class collisions. Constructor and modelling function names remain
concise because the package namespace already disambiguates functions; the
prefix is part of the underlying S3 class and method contract.

Printed objects use concise natural-language headings, such as "Parameter
specification", rather than presenting a second class-like name. Public
predicates remove the prefix and add `is_`: for example,
`is_parameter_spec(x)` tests for a parameter specification, while
`is_model(x)` tests the shared model superclass.
Direct calls to `inherits()` remain available when the technical class name is
needed.

Implementation anchor: every persistent model representation inherits from
`compphysiol_model`; the authored form has class
`compphysiol_compartment_model`, and executable forms additionally inherit from
`compphysiol_executable_model`.

## Process model

A process model is the package-owned intermediate representation of the
explicit process system obtained from a compartment model. It sits between the
modular compartment/molecule representation and downstream deterministic or
stochastic renderings.

Lowering a compartment model to a process model resolves wildcard wiring,
applies the state representation policy where possible, and expands
implementation structures such as infusion depots. The result has a
one-dimensional state vector, flattened dosing events, and a process list with
a stoichiometric matrix.

Each row of the process list stores the deterministic process rate, the
original constant expression for elementary/linear processes or `NA` for
explicit `rate = ...` definitions, and the input state indices with their
stoichiometries. The stoichiometric matrix maps these process rates onto state
derivatives. This keeps enough information to derive ODE right-hand sides and,
for supported elementary cases, future stochastic propensities.

For amount-state reactions in compartments with known volume, the process rate
is represented as an amount-change rate. Concentration-state reactions in an
unspecified volume can still be represented for deterministic ODE export, but
are not directly suitable for stochastic export.

Implementation anchor: `to_process_model()` creates
`compphysiol_process_model` objects.

## ODE model

An ODE model is the package-owned intermediate representation of a concrete
ODE system. It sits between the modular compartment model and a
solver-specific export such as a `deSolve` model.

Lowering a compartment model to an ODE model resolves wildcard wiring,
applies the ODE state representation policy, and expands implementation
structures such as infusion depots. After this step, the state structure is a
one-dimensional ODE state vector. Each state still has its DSL state name, such
as `a[drug, Central]`, but expressions in the internal representation refer to
states by index. This makes the representation independent of solver-specific
state naming conventions.

An ODE model stores initial value expressions, right-hand-side expressions,
equations, observables, parameters, free parameter names, state metadata, and
flattened dosing events. Expressions may still be symbolic and unit-aware.
Parameters already defined by the compartment model are carried into the
ODE model; other symbols remain free parameters to be supplied later, for
example during simulation.

Observables in an ODE model are still defined in terms of the model state, not
in terms of a solver output table. When an observable requests a concentration
state but the ODE state is represented as an amount, the lowered observable
uses the amount state together with the compartment volume conversion.

Unit checking remains a boundary operation rather than a defining part of the
representation. When the user supplies a compartment model, unit errors can be
reported in terms of compartments, transports, reactions, and other model
components. When the user supplies an ODE model, unit errors are reported in
terms of ODE states and their expressions.

An ODE model can also be lowered to a
compiled deSolve model. This does not change the mathematical
model; it prepares a deSolve-specific executable representation of the same ODE
system so that repeated numerical simulations can avoid rebuilding
solver-facing functions and metadata.

Implementation anchor: `to_ode_model()` creates `compphysiol_ode_model`
objects; `to_compiled_ode_model()` creates
`compphysiol_desolve_compiled_model` objects.

## ODE export

ODE export turns an ODE model into objects that can be used by an ODE solver.
This step prepares numeric initial conditions, substitutes equations and
parameters where needed, checks that all required numerical values are
available, handles dosing events, and builds the generated derivative function.

Conceptually, this is the point where the solver-neutral ODE description
becomes a solver-facing dynamical system. The amount-preferred state
representation policy described under State has already been applied when
creating the ODE model.

ODE export is a solver-facing boundary. The exported initial values, event
tables, and derivative functions are numeric objects in the requested output
dimensions, suitable for tools such as `deSolve`. Unit-aware model values are
converted and stripped for this purpose. Parametrized initial values must be
resolved by model or simulation parameters before this boundary can produce the
numeric initial state vector. The export result is therefore not the preferred
object for unit-aware downstream analysis.

Solver-facing exports preserve the conventions of the target solver. For
example, `deSolve` event tables are returned as raw event data, and output rows
that coincide with event times may follow `deSolve`'s event-time convention
rather than the toolbox-level simulation convention.

Implementation anchor: solver-specific ODE export is handled internally.
Users should call `simulate()` for solver output or `to_ode_model()` for the
solver-neutral ODE representation.

Compiled deSolve execution uses a cached solver-specific executable model. A
compiled deSolve model stores the original ODE model together with a compiled
right-hand side, compiled initial-value evaluation, fixed solver dimensions,
default dosing event data, and cached unit/output metadata. Runtime parameter
values and experiment dosing schedules may vary, but the parameter interface,
solver dimensions, and state/process structure are fixed once the compiled cache
has been created. Experiment dosing can only address existing amount states,
including the auxiliary states needed for infusions. Compartment-model simulation
prepares the union of infusion auxiliaries when given several experiments.

## Simulation

Simulation runs a compartment model or one of its lowered model
representations over requested time points and returns a toolbox-level result.
For compartment model inputs, the `simulation_type` argument selects the
route: numerical ODE simulation, analytical deterministic simulation,
Gillespie stochastic simulation, or Alfonsi hybrid stochastic-deterministic
simulation. Lowered ODE model, compiled deSolve model, analytical model, and
stochastic model objects can be simulated directly when repeated runs should
avoid repeated lowering or repeated ODE export work. Unlike ODE export,
simulation owns both sides of the solver boundary: it converts unit-aware model
quantities to numeric values for the solver and attaches units back to the
returned trajectories.

Hybrid simulation uses the same count-based stochastic model representation
as Gillespie simulation. A partition marks reactions as stochastic or
deterministic, either by a fixed logical vector or by an adaptive propensity
threshold. Stochastic event times can optionally be included in stochastic
simulation output for diagnostics; by default, stochastic and hybrid routes
report only the requested simulation times.

Stochastic and hybrid simulation can also limit the number of stochastic
reaction events per realization. This is a computational guardrail for models
whose stochastic event rate is too high for practical direct event simulation;
deterministic integration steps in a hybrid simulation are not counted as
stochastic events.

Simulation returns ODE state trajectories in a simulation result object.
When observables are defined, their predictions are included in an
observation data object
with `time`, `observable`, and `value` columns (plus `rep` for stochastic
replicates); otherwise the observables component is `NULL`. Direct time input
requests all observables at each time. An explicit experiment requests only its
scheduled pairs, preserving order and duplicate observation rows. ODE state
trajectories remain rectangular; experiment state output includes the initial
time and the sorted unique observation times.

Observable values are numeric for unit-free output, an ordinary `units` vector
when all units are identical, and a `mixed_units` column otherwise.
`as_observables_long()` exposes this table. `as_observables_wide()` produces one
ordinary unit-bearing or numeric column per observable, converting compatible
units within a column and filling absent combinations with typed missing values.
It rejects duplicate time-observable keys (within a replicate) instead of
aggregating. Both helpers accept an observable data frame directly, as well as
a simulation result, so users can subset the long table before widening without
modifying the result. This interface isolates downstream workflows from
mixed-unit storage.

At requested time points that coincide with dosing events, simulation reports
the post-event state. For example, a bolus dose at time zero appears in the
state trajectory at time zero. observables are calculated from the same
post-event states.

The `dimensions` argument controls the solver-facing numerical scale in
unit-aware simulations. Unit-bearing quantities are converted to plain numbers
in these dimensions before calling the ODE solver. This matters for numerical
tolerances: an absolute tolerance such as `atol` is interpreted on the internal
solver scale, which may differ from the units shown again in the returned
trajectories.

Simulation has two working modes with respect to time. In unit-free mode, the
model has no time units and simulation time is numeric. In unit-aware mode, the
model contains a time dimension, for example through a rate constant or dosing
time, and simulation time must carry compatible units, either directly in the
unit shorthand or through the `unit` argument. Mixed time modes are rejected: a
model with time units cannot be simulated with unit-free time points, and
unit-aware time points cannot be used with a model that is unit-free in time.

Passing a lowered model representation to `simulate()` can avoid repeated
lowering when the same model structure is simulated multiple times with
different runtime parameter values. Passing a compartment model keeps
diagnostics closer to the original model components.

Passing a compiled deSolve model goes further: after the first simulation fills the
compiled cache, repeated simulations reuse the compiled ODE representation and
cached solver metadata. This is intended for workloads such as parameter
estimation where the model structure is fixed and only parameter values vary.
Because the compiled cache fixes the solver dimensions and parameter interface,
later simulations must use compatible parameter units and cannot introduce
additional parameters or a different solver dimension set.

An rxode2 executable model follows the same cache principle: its generated and
compiled model, parameter interface, solver dimensions, observable functions,
events, and unit/output metadata are reused after the first simulation. When an
experiment collection is simulated with `rxode2_engine()`, each experiment is
an independent individual and the collection is executed in one batched
`rxSolve()` call. The returned value is one simulation result whose state and
observable tables carry experiment identifiers in collection order. This is a
simulation concern and does not require nlmixr2;
nlmixr2 enters when population estimation semantics are requested.

Experiment constructors establish the structural validity of experiments and
experiment collections. Methods such as collection subsetting and simulation
trust objects carrying those S3 classes rather than repeating full constructor
validation. Simulation still checks requirements that depend on the selected
model or execution request, including nonempty observation schedules, known
observable names, available parameters, dosing targets, and solver-boundary
unit compatibility.

Implementation anchor: simulation is handled by `simulate()` methods for
`compphysiol_compartment_model`, `compphysiol_ode_model`,
`compphysiol_desolve_compiled_model`, `compphysiol_rxode2_model`,
`compphysiol_analytical_model`, and `compphysiol_stochastic_model` objects; results use
`compphysiol_simulation_result`.

## Lumping

Lumping reduces a model by aggregating compartments or states while preserving
selected behaviour of the original model. In PBPK modelling, this is often used
to simplify a detailed model into a smaller model while retaining relevant
kinetic properties.

In `compphysiol`, lumping is more than renaming compartments. It changes the
state structure, combines initial conditions, removes transports that become
internal to a lumped group, and rewrites transport constants with appropriate
normalizing terms. Current lumping support is focused on linear models and
amount states.

Implementation anchor: lumping is handled by `lump_model()` and related
symbolic lumping helpers.

## Analytical representation

Some linear models can be converted to analytical representations rather than
being simulated only through numerical ODE integration. This is useful for
closed-form reasoning, model reduction, and comparison with classical PK
solutions.

An analytical model is the package-owned intermediate representation of a
linear system derived from a process model. It stores the system in the form
`dx/dt = A x + b`, together with the one-dimensional state metadata, initial
value expressions, equations, observables, parameters, and free parameter
names. The constant source term `b` is part of the representation, although
the first implementation only accepts homogeneous systems with `b = 0`.

Implementation anchor: `to_analytical_model()` creates
`compphysiol_analytical_model` objects that can be simulated with `simulate()`. Exporting
analytical solution functions is an internal compatibility path.
